description: Made-up situations with scenario-specific requests, formats and preferences.

scenarios.title: An email I have rewritten six times

situations.label: Late reply
situations.text: I owe a colleague a reply. They asked on Monday whether I could cover their Thursday meeting. I can join the first 20 minutes, but I have another commitment after that. I keep writing a whole paragraph to say this.

situations.label: Missing information
situations.text: I need to ask someone to send the room number and start time for a training session. They have already sent me a long email about the agenda, so I do not want this to sound like I ignored it.

situations.label: Change of plan
situations.text: We said we would send our team update on Friday. We are still checking two figures and can send it Tuesday instead. I want to explain the delay without making it sound like a catastrophe.

requests.label: Clear reply
requests.instruction: Help me write a clear, friendly reply.

requests.label: Short reply
requests.instruction: Help me say what needs saying without overexplaining.

requests.label: Natural reply
requests.instruction: Can you draft something that sounds like a person I would actually work with?

formats.label: One draft
formats.instruction: Give me one version I can edit.

formats.label: Two lengths
formats.instruction: Give me a short version and a slightly warmer one.

formats.label: Opening first
formats.instruction: Put the most useful sentence first.

constraints: Keep it under 100 words.
Please skip phrases like “I hope this finds you well.”
No grand apologies or promises I have not made.

scenarios.title: A handout that needs a human translation

situations.label: Arrival note
situations.text: I help with visitor information. Our draft says, “Upon arrival at the education room, attendees should present their registration confirmation to the session facilitator.” It just means bring your confirmation and show it to the person leading the class.

situations.label: Parking note
situations.text: I am updating directions for a staff class. The source says, “Participants utilizing the west lot should proceed via the courtyard entrance.” That is a lot of words for “Park in the west lot and come through the courtyard entrance.”

situations.label: Sign-in note
situations.text: Our volunteer orientation note says, “Individuals who have not completed the attendance verification process must report to the designated registration station.” The registration table is beside the classroom door.

requests.label: Plain words
requests.instruction: Rewrite this so someone can understand it on the first read.

requests.label: Helpful tone
requests.instruction: Make this clear and welcoming without adding new instructions.

requests.label: Explain edit
requests.instruction: Show me a clearer version and briefly explain the biggest change.

formats.label: One line
formats.instruction: Aim for one or two short sentences.

formats.label: Sign copy
formats.instruction: Make the wording suitable for a small sign.

formats.label: Two options
formats.instruction: Give me two options so I can pick the one that fits.

constraints: Use only the details I gave you.
Keep the original meaning intact.
Assume the reader is busy, not unfamiliar with life.

scenarios.title: The next shift should not have to guess

situations.label: Housekeeping
situations.text: I am finishing a housekeeping shift. These are my notes: supply cart restocked; replacement wheel requested for the other cart; training room still in use when I left; I have not heard back about the wheel. Help me leave something clearer for the next shift.

situations.label: Nursing admin
situations.text: I am a nurse tidying up our non-patient shift notes. The team printer is working again, the spare label rolls are in the usual drawer, and tomorrow's staff huddle moved to 8:15. The room for the huddle is still unconfirmed.

situations.label: Front desk
situations.text: I am handing over the welcome desk. We have enough visitor maps for today, tomorrow's delivery is not confirmed, and a caller asked us to check whether the education room has a hearing loop. Nobody has verified that yet.

requests.label: Clear handoff
requests.instruction: Turn these notes into a useful handoff.

requests.label: Open items
requests.instruction: Make it easy to see what is done and what still needs attention.

requests.label: Next shift
requests.instruction: Help the next person know where to pick up.

formats.label: Three bullets
formats.instruction: Keep it to a few bullets.

formats.label: Done and open
formats.instruction: Use “Done” and “Still open” if that helps.

formats.label: Read aloud
formats.instruction: Write it so I could read it aloud in under a minute.

constraints: Do not assign an owner unless I named one.
Keep unanswered questions visibly unanswered.
Please do not turn this into a project report.

scenarios.title: The supply cupboard treasure hunt

situations.label: Labels
situations.text: I work in environmental services. We have three shelves of everyday supplies, but people keep asking where things are. The labels use old names, new boxes go wherever they fit, and night staff are not around when we reorganize.

situations.label: Reordering
situations.text: Our front desk runs out of map leaflets even though we have a stock cupboard. One person notices we are low, another orders them, and nobody is sure whether an order has already gone in.

situations.label: Shared equipment
situations.text: I look after shared meeting supplies. We have enough adapters and markers, but they disappear into different rooms. People borrow them, leave them there, and the next person starts looking from scratch.

requests.label: Small improvement
requests.instruction: Help me find one small change we could try.

requests.label: Understand first
requests.instruction: Help me describe where the confusion happens before suggesting a fix.

requests.label: Ideas
requests.instruction: Suggest a few practical ways to make this less annoying.

formats.label: Quick note
formats.instruction: Give me a short note I can take to our team huddle.

formats.label: Simple steps
formats.instruction: Use a few practical steps, not a big rollout plan.

formats.label: Questions first
formats.instruction: Include two questions to ask the people who use the supplies.

constraints: Assume we have no budget for a new system.
Keep it workable for people on different shifts.
Do not change any safety or handling procedure.

scenarios.title: A slightly less chaotic lunch rush

situations.label: Queue confusion
situations.text: I work in a cafeteria. Three comments from this week: “I could not tell where to queue,” “I only wanted a drink but stood in the hot-food line,” and “The sign made sense once I reached the counter.”

situations.label: Menu visibility
situations.text: At our cafe, a customer said the menu was hard to read from the queue. Another asked whether the display was today's menu, and a third said they did not see prices until they reached the till.

situations.label: Tray return
situations.text: We are trying to make tray return easier. Staff have heard: “I could not see where trays go,” “I followed someone else,” and “There was a sign, but people standing nearby blocked it.”

requests.label: Themes
requests.instruction: What do these comments have in common?

requests.label: Ideas
requests.instruction: Suggest a small improvement we could try during one shift.

requests.label: Team discussion
requests.instruction: Help me turn this into a constructive team discussion.

formats.label: Huddle note
formats.instruction: Give me a short huddle note.

formats.label: One small trial
formats.instruction: Include one thing to try and one way to notice whether it helps.

formats.label: Three bullets
formats.instruction: Keep the answer to three or four useful bullets.

constraints: Do not generalize three comments into what everyone thinks.
Use a practical, friendly tone.
Keep food handling and allergen advice out of this; the issue is finding information.

scenarios.title: Teach me without making me feel daft

situations.label: Percentages
situations.text: I keep mixing up percent and percentage points. Our response rate went from 40% to 50%, and someone called that a 25% increase. I can follow the arithmetic once someone explains it, but I want it to stick.

situations.label: Median
situations.text: I help with a monthly report. Our five waiting times in minutes are 2, 3, 4, 5 and 26. I do not really understand why the average and median tell such different stories.

situations.label: Rates
situations.text: I am looking at two teams' training completions. One completed 18 out of 20; the other completed 27 out of 30. The second team did more, but the completion rates are the same. Help me explain the difference.

requests.label: Teach
requests.instruction: Walk me through this in plain language.

requests.label: Example
requests.instruction: Use my numbers to explain the idea.

requests.label: Check understanding
requests.instruction: Explain it, then ask me one question to check I understand.

formats.label: Short lesson
formats.instruction: Keep the first explanation under 150 words.

formats.label: Step by step
formats.instruction: Show one small step at a time.

formats.label: Memory aid
formats.instruction: Include a simple way to remember the distinction.

constraints: No unexplained jargon.
Assume I am curious, just out of practice.
Please use these numbers rather than adding a complicated example.

scenarios.title: Someone new starts Monday

situations.label: Reception
situations.text: A new colleague is joining our reception team. I can show them the desk and introduce people, but I want them to know how to ask for help without feeling they should remember everything on day one.

situations.label: Food service
situations.text: I am helping a new cafeteria colleague settle in. Their formal training is already arranged. I want a friendly first-day guide covering introductions, where to find the rota, and who to ask when a question comes up.

situations.label: Analyst
situations.text: A new business analyst joins our team next week. There are dozens of old documents, and I do not want their welcome message to be a wall of links. I want a sensible way to introduce the people and current work.

requests.label: Welcome
requests.instruction: Help me draft a simple welcome plan.

requests.label: First day
requests.instruction: What should we cover on day one and what can wait?

requests.label: Starter guide
requests.instruction: Help me outline a useful first-day guide.

formats.label: One page
formats.instruction: Make it something that would fit on one page.

formats.label: Conversation
formats.instruction: Write it as prompts for a welcoming conversation.

formats.label: Before and after
formats.instruction: Split it into “Before they arrive” and “On the day.”

constraints: Leave local names and locations as blanks for me to fill in.
Keep formal training separate from my informal welcome.
Make it friendly without being relentlessly cheerful.

scenarios.title: A conversation I would rather not wing

situations.label: Interruptions
situations.text: A colleague often answers questions directed at me in our meetings. I do not think they mean harm, but I end up not getting a turn. I want to raise it privately without making it a bigger thing than it needs to be.

situations.label: Late inputs
situations.text: I manage a small team. One colleague has sent their part of our weekly update late three weeks in a row. I do not know what is getting in the way, and I want to ask before assuming they do not care.

situations.label: Extra work
situations.text: People keep asking me to add “one quick thing” near the end of my shift. Sometimes I can help, sometimes I cannot. I want a polite way to explain what I can finish and what needs to wait.

requests.label: Opening
requests.instruction: Help me find a natural way to start this conversation.

requests.label: Rehearse
requests.instruction: Give me a possible opening and a couple of ways the conversation might go.

requests.label: Clear ask
requests.instruction: Help me say what I have noticed and make a reasonable request.

formats.label: Talking points
formats.instruction: Use talking points, not a script I have to memorize.

formats.label: Short opening
formats.instruction: Keep the opening to two or three sentences.

formats.label: One question
formats.instruction: Include a question that leaves room for their perspective.

constraints: Do not guess what the other person is thinking.
Keep it calm and direct.
Avoid management-speak.

scenarios.title: There is a pattern in here somewhere

situations.label: Training comments
situations.text: After a staff class, we got four comments: “Useful examples,” “Too fast near the end,” “More time to try it myself,” and “I liked the short format.” I want to use these without assuming everyone wants a longer class.

situations.label: Meeting comments
situations.text: Our team tried a shorter meeting. Feedback was: “Loved getting the time back,” “I missed hearing from the other shift,” “The written notes helped,” and “I forgot to read the notes.”

situations.label: Form comments
situations.text: We tried a simpler internal form. Three people said it was quicker. One said they could not find where to explain an unusual case. Another said they preferred the old form because they knew it already.

requests.label: Themes
requests.instruction: Help me sort the main themes and differences.

requests.label: Next attempt
requests.instruction: Suggest one change for the next attempt.

requests.label: Review
requests.instruction: What can we reasonably conclude, and what is still a guess?

formats.label: Brief note
formats.instruction: Give me a brief note for the people who helped.

formats.label: Try next
formats.instruction: End with one thing to try next.

formats.label: Balanced summary
formats.instruction: Keep the summary short, including the conflicting views.

constraints: Do not turn a handful of comments into a survey statistic.
Use the actual comments rather than inventing quotes.
Keep the tone curious, not defensive.

scenarios.title: Help me choose without a 40-slide deck

situations.label: Class slots
situations.text: We can offer a staff class twice for 12 people each time, or once for 24. Two sessions cost us an extra hour of teaching time but give shift workers another chance to attend. We have not asked staff which time works yet.

situations.label: Equipment
situations.text: We need a shared display for a small training room. Option A costs 400 and is portable; option B costs 650 and stays mounted. We use the room twice a week and sometimes teach elsewhere. These are practice figures, not quotes.

situations.label: Leadership choice
situations.text: I need to brief our leadership team on two ways to share routine updates: a weekly 20-minute call or a written note with an optional monthly discussion. We have colleagues on three different schedules and no data yet on what they prefer.

requests.label: Compare
requests.instruction: Help me compare these options against what matters here.

requests.label: Recommendation
requests.instruction: Give me a tentative recommendation and what could change your mind.

requests.label: Missing facts
requests.instruction: Help me see which missing facts would actually affect the decision.

formats.label: Small table
formats.instruction: Use a small comparison table.

formats.label: Brief advice
formats.instruction: Make it a short recommendation I can read before a meeting.

formats.label: Decision note
formats.instruction: Give me the tradeoff, the uncertainty and the next question.

constraints: Do not invent savings or popularity figures.
Include an alternative only if it adds something useful.
Please do not make this sound more complicated than it is.

scenarios.title: Read this little study with me

situations.label: Training study
situations.text: Here is a made-up abstract for practice: 30 staff chose either a live class or a recorded lesson. Average quiz scores were 8/10 for the live group and 7/10 for the recording group. No baseline quiz was given, and staff chose their own group. The authors say live teaching is better.

situations.label: Reminder study
situations.text: Practice abstract: A team sent a new reminder email for one month. Attendance was 18/20 that month and 14/20 the previous month. The topic and attendees differed between months. The authors suggest the new reminder improved attendance.

situations.label: Checklist study
situations.text: Practice abstract: Eight volunteers tried a new checklist and all said it was easy to use. There was no comparison checklist and no measurement of mistakes or time. The authors conclude that the checklist improves performance.

requests.label: Explain
requests.instruction: Explain what this study does and does not show.

requests.label: Critique
requests.instruction: Help me read the conclusion with a reasonably skeptical eye.

requests.label: Teach
requests.instruction: Use this as a short lesson in reading research.

formats.label: Reading note
formats.instruction: Give me a compact reading note.

formats.label: Three questions
formats.instruction: Include three questions I would want the full paper to answer.

formats.label: Plain summary
formats.instruction: Write it for a curious colleague who does not read research every day.

constraints: Work only from the abstract I supplied.
Do not invent a real citation for this practice study.
Keep uncertainty visible without dismissing the whole study.

scenarios.title: Make this meeting earn its place

situations.label: Team huddle
situations.text: I have 15 minutes with our team. We need to choose a time for next month's training, flag a supply issue and hear one suggestion from the evening shift. The last few huddles ran long because we started solving every issue on the spot.

situations.label: Committee
situations.text: Our committee has 30 minutes to review two ideas for welcoming new staff and decide who will gather feedback. We already sent the background note. I would rather spend the time deciding than reading it aloud.

situations.label: IT update
situations.text: I am preparing a 20-minute update with our technology lead. We need a decision about which of two internal tools to review first. The two owners can each give a brief overview, but we do not need a live demo.

requests.label: Agenda
requests.instruction: Help me build a focused agenda.

requests.label: Keep time
requests.instruction: Help me keep the discussion on track without cutting people off.

requests.label: Useful finish
requests.instruction: Make sure we end with a clear decision or next step.

formats.label: Time boxes
formats.instruction: Use a few agenda items with time allowances.

formats.label: Chair notes
formats.instruction: Give me brief notes I can use while leading it.

formats.label: Invitation
formats.instruction: Draft a short agenda I can put in the invitation.

constraints: Stay within the time I gave you.
Keep the language conversational.
Leave names unassigned where I have not given them.

scenarios.title: A day with too many moving parts

situations.label: Nurse admin
situations.text: I am a nurse with a protected hour for admin. I need to review a ten-minute training video by Friday, send tomorrow's huddle reminder, and finish a 20-minute draft of our welcome sheet. It is Wednesday, and people may interrupt.

situations.label: Physician teaching
situations.text: I am a physician preparing for a staff teaching session. I have 45 minutes today to outline the talk, reply about the room setup, and find out how many people are coming. The session is next week. This is planning time, not patient care.

situations.label: Office tasks
situations.text: I have 40 minutes before lunch. I need to send the meeting agenda for tomorrow, tidy a draft that will take about 20 minutes, and check whether someone replied about next month's room booking. I keep bouncing between all three.

requests.label: Priority
requests.instruction: Help me decide what to do first.

requests.label: Time plan
requests.instruction: Make me a realistic plan for the time I have.

requests.label: Smaller start
requests.instruction: Help me make a start without trying to finish everything.

formats.label: Short list
formats.instruction: Keep it to a short ordered list.

formats.label: Time blocks
formats.instruction: Use rough time blocks with room for interruptions.

formats.label: Now and later
formats.instruction: Split it into “Now” and “Can wait.”

constraints: Do not invent deadlines for things that do not have one.
Keep the plan flexible.
Give me one clear first step.

scenarios.title: A small gathering, not a military operation

situations.label: Welcome coffee
situations.text: We want a 20-minute welcome coffee for three new colleagues. About 12 people may come, we have a usual break room, and we need to check whether the evening shift can join. No catering has been arranged.

situations.label: Show and tell
situations.text: I am organizing a lunchtime show-and-tell where four colleagues each share a useful tip. We have 40 minutes and a room with a display. I still need to confirm who can attend.

situations.label: Volunteer thanks
situations.text: Our team wants a short thank-you gathering for our volunteers. We expect about 15 people, have a half-hour slot, and want it to feel personal. We have not picked a room or refreshments yet.

requests.label: Checklist
requests.instruction: Help me make a small planning checklist.

requests.label: Run of show
requests.instruction: Suggest a simple order for the gathering.

requests.label: Invite
requests.instruction: Draft a friendly invitation with blanks for the unconfirmed details.

formats.label: Short
formats.instruction: Keep it brief enough to use without another planning meeting.

formats.label: Open details
formats.instruction: Make the things I still need to confirm easy to spot.

formats.label: First steps
formats.instruction: Include the first two things I should do.

constraints: Do not assume everyone can attend at the same time.
Do not make bookings or promises.
Keep it proportionate to a small gathering.

scenarios.title: Help me say this in another language

situations.label: Class welcome
situations.text: I am preparing a draft sign for a staff class in English and Spanish. The English text is: “Welcome. Please write your name on a badge and take any open seat. We will start at 9.”

situations.label: Volunteer note
situations.text: I need a Spanish draft of this volunteer event note: “Thank you for joining us. The welcome table is beside the main entrance. Please ask there if you need directions.”

situations.label: Feedback sign
situations.text: I would like a Spanish draft of this sign for a staff workshop: “Tell us what helped and what we could improve. You can leave your comment without your name.”

requests.label: Translate
requests.instruction: Translate the supplied text into natural Spanish.

requests.label: Both versions
requests.instruction: Show the English and Spanish together.

requests.label: Wording choices
requests.instruction: Translate it and mention any wording choice worth checking.

formats.label: Sign length
formats.instruction: Keep it suitable for a small sign.

formats.label: Copy ready
formats.instruction: Give me text I can copy into a draft.

formats.label: Review note
formats.instruction: Add a brief note for the person who will review the wording.

constraints: Preserve the details in the original.
This will get a language review before use.
Use a welcoming, straightforward tone.

scenarios.title: Surely I should not have to copy this twice

situations.label: Attendance
situations.text: I copy the date and class name from our training list into a weekly summary every Friday. The list is a spreadsheet with Date, Class and Attendee count. I want to explore a simpler way before building anything.

situations.label: Room requests
situations.text: I receive room requests with three fields: day, time and expected attendance. I then copy those fields into a planning sheet. It is repetitive, but the source messages are not always formatted the same way.

situations.label: Supply summary
situations.text: I have a small stock sheet with Item, Count and Reorder level. Each week I manually list the items below their reorder level. I would like help making that step easier to repeat.

requests.label: Approach
requests.instruction: Help me choose the simplest workable approach.

requests.label: Understand
requests.instruction: First help me describe the rule and the exceptions.

requests.label: Trial
requests.instruction: Suggest a small test using made-up data.

formats.label: Plain outline
formats.instruction: Give me a plain-language outline before any code.

formats.label: Example
formats.instruction: Show one tiny input and the expected output.

formats.label: Questions
formats.instruction: Include only the questions that affect the approach.

constraints: Do not assume a particular software license or connector.
Do not connect to any real system for this example.
Keep unusual or incomplete inputs visible instead of silently dropping them.

scenarios.title: Which request am I supposed to use?

situations.label: Broken chair
situations.text: The height adjustment on our office chair no longer holds. I want to find the right request for a repair or replacement, but the service portal has a lot of categories and I am not sure where to start.

situations.label: New starter
situations.text: A colleague starts in three weeks and will need a computer and access to a shared team folder. I know these may be separate requests, but I do not know the correct catalog items.

situations.label: Printer problem
situations.text: The shared printer in our staff workroom keeps jamming. I want to report it with enough detail that the receiving team does not have to start by asking all the obvious questions.

requests.label: Find route
requests.instruction: Help me work out which request to look for and what details to gather.

requests.label: Draft
requests.instruction: Help me prepare a clear request and identify the missing fields.

requests.label: Search terms
requests.instruction: Give me useful portal search terms and a short question to ask the service desk if I get stuck.

formats.label: Short guide
formats.instruction: Keep it to a short guide I can use while looking at the portal.

formats.label: Copy ready
formats.instruction: Include a copy-ready description with blanks for missing facts.

formats.label: Steps
formats.instruction: Give me the next few steps in order.

constraints: I have not provided access to the live catalog, so do not invent a form name or link.
Treat catalog names and routing as unverified until we can inspect them.
For this example, prepare the request but do not submit anything.

scenarios.title: Three tickets, one thing I need done

situations.label: Provisioning
situations.text: I am setting up a server and three teams are involved. My notes say capacity is approved, network setup is waiting for an address range, and backup enrollment cannot begin until the server exists. These are practice notes; I have not given you live ticket access.

situations.label: Equipment chain
situations.text: A new colleague needs equipment and access. In this practice case, the computer request is marked approved, delivery has no date, and the access team says they need the device name before they can finish. I keep checking three places to see what is happening.

situations.label: Server move
situations.text: For a practice server move, the hosting team says the destination is ready, the network request is waiting for a confirmed move date, and the application owner has not agreed on a test window. I need a clearer picture of what is holding this up.

requests.label: Status
requests.instruction: Turn this into a short status update that makes the dependencies clear.

requests.label: Follow-up
requests.instruction: Show what is waiting on whom and draft the most useful follow-up question.

requests.label: Check routine
requests.instruction: Help me outline a daily status check: what to read, what counts as a change and when to notify me.

formats.label: Tracker
formats.instruction: Use a small tracker plus a two-sentence summary.

formats.label: Update
formats.instruction: Give me a brief update I could share after checking the facts.

formats.label: Next move
formats.instruction: End with the next useful action, not just “follow up.”

constraints: Do not invent ticket IDs, agreed dates or completed work.
Draft messages only; no contacting teams or configuring a schedule in this example.
Make it clear which facts still need a live check.

scenarios.title: An Ansible playbook I can understand

situations.label: Inventory
situations.text: I inherited an Ansible repository and want to understand which servers a playbook would target before anyone runs it. I have not attached the files yet. Help me work out what to inspect and what information you need.

situations.label: Service config
situations.text: I want help planning a small Ansible change to a service configuration on a test server. We have an existing playbook, but I have not shared the inventory, OS or service details yet. I want to start with a sensible review, not a guessed command.

situations.label: Patching
situations.text: I help manage a few servers and want to understand how an Ansible patching playbook could test one server before moving on. I have not supplied our current playbook or maintenance rules. This is a planning exercise.

requests.label: Walkthrough
requests.instruction: Walk me through a sensible starting point.

requests.label: Review checklist
requests.instruction: Give me a short checklist for reviewing the existing setup.

requests.label: Working session
requests.instruction: Help me prepare for a working session with the person who owns the repository.

formats.label: Beginner friendly
formats.instruction: Explain any Ansible terms you use.

formats.label: Concise
formats.instruction: Keep the first response focused on the next few steps.

formats.label: Concrete
formats.instruction: Distinguish what we can inspect locally from what needs server access.

constraints: Do not assume production access or invent an inventory.
Do not run commands against servers in this example.
Call out what a check-mode result could leave untested.

scenarios.title: We must have figured this out before

situations.label: Old guide
situations.text: We are updating a welcome guide. I have last year's draft, notes from two team meetings and a list of corrections someone emailed. I want help finding which decisions are still unresolved before rewriting it.

situations.label: Past trial
situations.text: Our team once tried a different stock-check routine. I have the original idea and a short recap, but the recap mixes what happened with what people hoped would happen. I want to learn from it without overstating the result.

situations.label: Repeated question
situations.text: People keep asking how we decided on our current meeting format. I have an old agenda and two sets of notes. I would like help tracing the decision instead of relying on whoever remembers loudest.

requests.label: Evidence map
requests.instruction: Help me organize the sources and the questions to answer.

requests.label: Read carefully
requests.instruction: Show how to separate a recorded decision from a suggestion.

requests.label: Keep lesson
requests.instruction: Help me identify what might be worth keeping for next time.

formats.label: Small note
formats.instruction: Start with a short reading plan.

formats.label: Source table
formats.instruction: Use a small table of sources, possible answers and gaps.

formats.label: Ask next
formats.instruction: End with what you need me to share first.

constraints: I have described the sources but have not supplied them yet.
Do not claim to know what the missing documents say.
Keep uncertain recollections separate from recorded decisions.

scenarios.title: Let me show you what I mean

situations.label: Business analyst
situations.text: I am a business analyst trying to explain a better way to request a shared room. People keep interpreting my written description differently. I want a simple screen with a date, time, group size and a place to explain an unusual request.

situations.label: Frontline idea
situations.text: I work at a welcome desk and have an idea for a clearer visitor information sheet. Instead of explaining it in another meeting, I want to show a sample with an arrival note, a small directions area and a place for a contact number.

situations.label: Manager idea
situations.text: I manage a small team. I want to show what a simpler weekly update might look like: what changed, what needs a decision and what is coming next. Our current version is a long email that people skim.

requests.label: First version
requests.instruction: Make me a small first version that people can react to.

requests.label: Try it
requests.instruction: Help me turn this into something I can inspect and tweak.

requests.label: Learn by doing
requests.instruction: Build a simple example and explain one useful design choice as we go.

formats.label: Minimal
formats.instruction: Keep it small enough to understand at a glance.

formats.label: Editable
formats.instruction: Use an editable format if your tools support it.

formats.label: Show difference
formats.instruction: Make the improvement visible without a long explanation.

constraints: Use made-up details and mark anything simulated.
Do not connect to real services or publish it.
Treat this as a conversation starter, not a finished product.

scenarios.title: I want to make sense of this reading pile

situations.label: New topic
situations.text: I want to understand composting before our neighborhood starts a shared bin. I have a few public guides, and the confident advice does not always agree.

situations.label: Manual pile
situations.text: I am helping at a community repair event and have three public equipment manuals. I want to understand what each one covers before I try to explain anything.

situations.label: Teach something back
situations.text: I am putting together a five-minute talk on local history for a community group. I have a few public articles and more enthusiasm than structure.

requests.label: Notebook first steps
requests.instruction: Help me plan a small Gemini Notebook exercise using public sources. Explain what to add and give me a useful first question. If I cannot access it, offer an approach in my approved assistant.

requests.label: See the differences
requests.instruction: Help me ask where the sources agree, where they differ and what I should check in the originals. Do not pretend you have read material I have not supplied.

requests.label: Learn out loud
requests.instruction: Help me turn this into a short learning session with three questions I should be able to answer afterward.

formats.label: A small plan
formats.instruction: Give me three steps I can follow without a technical background.

formats.label: Questions to paste
formats.instruction: Give me a first question and two follow-ups I can paste into my assistant.

formats.label: A tiny walkthrough
formats.instruction: Walk me through a small invented example, clearly labeled as made up.

constraints: Use public material only and keep any work-account restrictions in view.
Help me trace one answer back to its source; I want to learn the habit, too.
Keep it friendly and short. I am curious, but I do not need homework about my homework.
